technique: entering mid-action, with no setup at all
poem:
The fog came down the hillside overnight
and lay in the low field like something kept,
then thinned — you watched it go, the way a hand
lets out a rope it's done with holding tight.
Wind took the maples next, a dry brown rush,
the kind of sound that means the warm's worn thin
and won't come back the same. Some things you squared
and would not bend on: you said no, and meant it,
and the saying cost you nothing but the morning.
Now the cold air stands clean above the rows,
each envelope of seed named, shelved, and still,
the whole year drawn in bars from here to here —

Everything you put down last night is still there,
sorted and holding its place — and the light's coming up now to meet it.

So — up!

Everything you put down last night is still there, sorted and holding its place — and the light's coming up now to meet it.

So — up!
lesson: Today we work on one technique, ending a poem with a direct command. Most of this poem describes things, the fog, the wind, the seeds on the shelf. It stays calm and quiet for a long time. Then the last line turns and speaks to you. It says so, up. That is an order. The word so ties it to everything before it. The dash makes you stop for a second. Then up tells you to do one thing, get up. Why it works, after many lines of looking at still things, a short command wakes you. Two words after twelve long lines feel loud. The order moves you from watching to acting. Try this, write six or more quiet describing lines, then end with a two word command that tells the reader to move. The second time through, listen for how, so, up, hits after you already know what came before.
